Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

BitChat is not a covert network. It is a Bluetooth mesh: nearby phones form a local cluster, and a message hops through other phones about seven hops, a few hundred metres in good conditions. No account. No phone number. No central server. Direct messages are end-to-end encrypted. Built for a crowd, a protest, a blackout, a disaster zone. Not city-wide messaging.
The public record of misuse is thin. The documented Indian spike is July 2026, around the Jantar Mantar protests. India briefly accounted for most of the app’s global downloads. The official line was “substantial risk of misuse.” No reported case of a serious offence is in the open record.
Police cannot do with this what they do with WhatsApp or a telecom operator. That fear can exist. It is not evidence the app has been used for a serious crime in India.
Section 69A lets the Centre order an intermediary to block public access to information on grounds such as security or public order. Apple’s notice says MeitY used it because the app “includes content that is illegal in India.” It does not name that content. The order has not been published.
The Court upheld 69A in Shreya Singhal only with safeguards: written reasons, a committee, a hearing, and a path to court. A secret whole-app removal is a different design.
Blocking the app, in secret, because it still works when the network is cut, is not the same as blocking a specific unlawful message. 🔪📵⚖️

On October 2nd, the government blocked BitChat in India without making the order public. We only found out through a notice on the iOS App Store.

BitChat uses Bluetooth mesh technology to pass messages from phone to phone. During Jantar Mantar 1.0, when the internet was shut and blocking vans jammed even SMS, protesters used it to find each other and share water and medicines.

Calling it a national security threat makes little sense. It only works over short distances, and the block only stops new downloads. Anyone can install it across the border and come back. The only people affected are citizens exercising their right to peaceful assembly.

What’s next, walkie-talkies and carrier pigeons? We’re filing RTIs and will keep pushing for transparency.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

🚨Elon Musk vs India’s Satellite Internet Market: Musk Targets Ambani

Elon Musk has publicly accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s entry into India in order to protect what he described as a “monopolistic chokehold” over consumers. Musk did not name Mukesh Ambani or Reliance Jio, but the backdrop makes the reference difficult to ignore: Reliance is preparing its own major push into low-Earth-orbit satellite connectivity, putting it directly in competition with Starlink.

This is not a new rivalry.

The Musk-Ambani confrontation over India’s satellite-internet market has been building for years. In 2023, Reuters reported that Reliance had pushed for satellite spectrum to be auctioned, while Starlink argued that spectrum should be administratively assigned. The disagreement was fundamentally about the rules under which foreign satellite companies would compete with Indian telecom operators.

Musk eventually won an important part of that policy battle when India moved toward administrative allocation of satellite spectrum rather than auctions. At the time, Reuters described the decision as potentially setting the stage for a price battle between Musk and Ambani.

But the competition has since become much bigger.

Reliance is no longer merely defending its telecom business. It is preparing for the satellite era itself. Jio is reportedly planning a constellation of roughly 1,600–1,650 low-Earth-orbit satellites, potentially providing broadband and direct-to-device connectivity.

Starlink, meanwhile, is pushing deeper into the Indian market. Its first-generation constellation received IN-SPACe approval in 2025, while the company has subsequently reapplied for approval for a much larger Gen 2 constellation with newer capabilities.

India is already one of the world's largest digital markets, but satellite connectivity could open another frontier by reaching remote villages, difficult terrain, ships, aircraft and locations where conventional fibre and mobile infrastructure remain expensive or impractical.

That makes India too important for Musk to ignore, and too strategically important for Indian telecom giants to surrender without a fight. However, looking at current prices of Starlink, the cost of Starlink   is way too costlier for Indian market. 

The irony is that Musk's latest accusation comes precisely as India is trying to construct the regulatory framework for this emerging industry. Starlink, Jio and other players still require spectrum allocation and various security and regulatory clearances before commercial satellite services can fully begin.

So the real battle is no longer simply Musk versus Ambani.

It is a battle over who gets to shape India's satellite-connectivity ecosystem, and under what rules.

He may not have named Ambani.

But in India's satellite-internet race, the two billionaires are already moving toward the same battlefield.

Nobody is driving. Nobody is stacking. And this is how most of what you own gets to you.

Read that again, because the scariest part of global trade is not how much of it moves. It's who moves it.

Not people. Software.

This is the story of the quietest revolution in human history. No keynote. No launch event. No billionaire on a stage holding a glowing rectangle. It happened one terminal at a time, over thirty years, at the edge of the sea, behind fences, where almost nobody looks.

And today it decides whether your next phone is on a shelf in November or floating in a queue until March.

This is a long one. Stay with me. By the end you will never look at a cardboard box the same way again.

01 / THE BOX THAT ATE THE WORLD

April 1956. A converted tanker called the Ideal X leaves Newark with 58 metal boxes on its deck. The man behind it is a trucking owner named Malcolm McLean, and the people who work the docks think he has lost his mind.

Here is the number that ended an era.

Loading loose cargo by hand cost roughly $5.86 per ton. Loading the same cargo in boxes cost roughly 16 cents.

That is not a 10 percent improvement. That is more than thirty times cheaper.

Read that again, because that is not optimization. That is a cost collapse so violent that entire waterfronts died inside a decade. Old piers emptied. Ports that could not make room for the boxes lost everything to ports that could. Jobs that had existed for centuries evaporated, and nobody voted on it.

Before the box, a ship could sit at a dock for a week while armies of men carried sacks, barrels and crates by hand and by hook. A ship only earns money while it moves. A ship in port is a very expensive piece of furniture.

After the box, the same ship is in and out in about a day.

The box made distance cheap. Cheap distance made one country the factory of the world. The factory of the world built the modern consumer economy. Your closet, your kitchen, your phone, your car, your kid's toys. All of it traces back to a steel rectangle and one man who refused to accept that loading a ship had to be slow.

But the box carried a hidden consequence that took fifty years to show up.

The box standardized the world.

And anything standardized, sooner or later, gets automated.

02 / A PORT IS NOT A PLACE. IT IS A COMPUTER.

Here is the thing that breaks people's brains when they first learn it.

A modern container terminal is not mainly cranes and concrete. Cranes and concrete are the hardware. The real product is a decision engine that answers one question millions of times a year.

Where should this box go, and when, so that the next box does not have to wait?

Sounds trivial. It is one of the nastiest scheduling problems in industry.

Picture a ship with ten thousand boxes aboard, each one headed for a different truck, train, warehouse or another ship. Every box has a destination, a weight, a deadline, a customs status, and sometimes a temperature it must not exceed. Now stack them in a yard where you can only reach the top one. If the box you need first is buried under six others, you have to move six boxes that nobody asked you to move. Logistics people call those wasted moves rehandles, and they are pure poison for the schedule.

So every placement is a bet on the future. Put this box here, and you are betting on which ship, which truck, which hour will want it. Bet wrong, and you pay in minutes. Minutes multiply across tens of thousands of boxes.

Humans used to make those bets with experience and gut feeling. A veteran planner who had worked the yard for twenty years could smell a bad stack.

Software now makes them faster, and it never gets tired, never gets distracted, never has a bad Monday.

The real revolution is not the machines you can see moving. It's the invisible layer of code that tells them where to go.

Think about what that means. A terminal is a factory whose raw material is time.

And factories whose raw material is time have a very simple rule: whoever wastes less of it wins.

03 / THE REVOLUTION NOBODY FILMED

The first automated container terminal with driverless vehicles opened in Rotterdam in 1993. Read the year again. Before most people had email.

For a long time, it stayed a curiosity. Expensive, slow to roll out, and politically radioactive. Operators in the West looked at the price tag and the union contracts and said: interesting, maybe later.

Then one country looked at the same technology and said: now.

China did not invent port automation. China did something scarier. It treated port automation as an industrial policy and built it at a scale that nobody else was willing to finance. In the last decade, new terminals went up with driverless electric vehicles, remote-controlled cranes and a single software brain coordinating all of it. Several of the world's busiest container ports sit in that country, and most of the global top ten are Chinese. Shanghai alone has handled on the order of fifty million containers a year.

Fifty million. A year. At one port.

Let that sink in for a second. For scale, the whole planet moves something like eight hundred million of these boxes annually. One city's harbor handles a slice that would have been unthinkable to the men who watched the Ideal X sail.

And here is the part that should keep you up at night.

Those vehicles do not get paid. They do not take breaks. They do not call in sick. They charge, they run, they charge again. They follow instructions with a consistency no human crew can match, because they are not following instructions at all. They are executing a plan that was computed seconds earlier by a system that knows where every other machine is.

Imagine a thousand-piece orchestra with no conductor visible, no sheet music on stage, no one counting beats. And somehow nobody ever plays a wrong note.

That is a modern automated terminal at 3 a.m.

Nobody is in the room. The room is the machine.

04 / THE LAST METER

Now for the plot twist that almost every article skips.

Even the most advanced terminal on Earth is not fully autonomous. Not even close.

Machines are brilliant at the repeatable parts. Drive from A to B. Lift a box. Set it down within a few centimeters. Do it again, nine hundred times a day.

Machines are still bad at the weird parts. A twist lock that is jammed. A container that is slightly damaged. A lashing that needs a person with a tool and a pair of eyes. A box that does not behave the way the model says it should.

Engineers have a name for this. They call it the last meter problem. The first 95 percent of any process is easy to automate. The last 5 percent is where all the money and all the pain are hiding.

So what happens in practice? The crane operator no longer climbs a ladder to a cab forty meters above the water. They sit in an air-conditioned office, hands on joysticks, watching screens, steering a crane that is miles away. One person can supervise what used to need several, and the job changes from athletic to cognitive.

Some call that progress. Others call it a slow-motion layoff with better chairs.

Both are right, and that is exactly why this is the most important labor story of the decade.

Because the question is not whether these jobs shrink. The question is how fast, and who gets to decide.

05 / THE PRICE OF A PERFECT MACHINE

Here is the dirty secret of efficiency.

The more perfectly a system runs, the less slack it has. And the less slack it has, the more violently it breaks.

A messy, human, old-fashioned port has friction everywhere. Delays, improvisation, workarounds, someone who knows a guy. All that mess acts like a shock absorber. When something goes wrong, the mess absorbs it.

A perfectly tuned automated terminal has no mess. Every minute is spoken for. Every machine is scheduled. Every gap has been squeezed out and sold.

That is gorgeous. Right up until the day it is not.

In June 2017, a piece of malware called NotPetya tore through the networks of one of the largest shipping companies in the world. It was not even aimed at them. It was collateral damage from a cyberattack on a different country. The company reportedly lost somewhere between 200 and 300 million dollars. Terminals stopped. Trucks lined up outside gates with nowhere to go. Thousands of computers and servers had to be rebuilt from scratch.

And how did they recover? Reportedly through one single machine in a remote office, in a different country, that happened to be offline because of a power cut on the day the malware spread. It survived by accident. One lucky blackout.

Think about that. A global giant, saved by a power outage.

In November 2023, another cyber incident hit a major port operator in Australia and froze terminals across the country for days. By most estimates, close to forty percent of the nation's freight was affected.

Same lesson, different continent.

The more software runs the dock, the more the dock becomes a target. A century ago, if you wanted to stop a port, you needed a strike or a storm. Today you need a stranger with a laptop and a good exploit.

And nobody put that on the brochure.

06 / THE DAY THE OCEAN HAD A TRAFFIC JAM

If you want to feel how thin the margin really is, look at what happens when a single node jams.

March 2021. One ship, one gust, one canal. A vessel called the Ever Given wedges itself across the Suez Canal and stays there for roughly six days. About twelve percent of global trade normally passes through that ditch. Estimates from the shipping press put the value of goods held up at around nine billion dollars a day.

Nine billion. Per day. Because of one parked boat.

Then the pandemic demand wave hit the other end of the chain, and the world got a live demonstration of what a stressed network looks like. At the peak, more than a hundred ships sat anchored off the California coast, waiting for a berth. Container prices on some routes jumped several times over. Furniture, bikes, appliances, electronics, parts for factories that were suddenly unable to finish a product because one tiny component was sitting on a ship in the Pacific.

People blamed greed. They blamed ports. They blamed workers. The real culprit was simpler and more uncomfortable.

The system had been optimized for a perfect world.

Just in time. No buffer. No spare capacity. Every asset running near its limit, because spare capacity looks like waste on a spreadsheet. And when reality stopped being perfect, the system had nowhere to bend.

Then in late 2023, ships began avoiding the Red Sea and taking the long way around Africa. That adds roughly a week or two to Asia to Europe voyages. A week or two, multiplied by thousands of vessels, quietly swallowed a chunk of the world's shipping capacity without anyone building or losing a single ship.

Distance is a resource. Time is a resource. And the whole planet has been quietly betting that neither would ever get scarce.

07 / WHY THE HARBOR IS THE REAL BATTLEFIELD

Strip away the politics and look at it like an engineer.

About eighty percent of world trade by volume goes by sea, according to the United Nations trade body. Most of the manufactured stuff in your life sits inside a box at some point on its journey. Ports are the narrowest part of that funnel. Everything passes through them. Everything.

Whoever runs the funnel has leverage over everyone who needs what comes through it.

That is why ports stopped being boring infrastructure and became strategic assets. Governments now argue over who is allowed to build them, who is allowed to buy stakes in them, and whose software is allowed to run inside them. Some terminals use equipment built in one country, operated by a company in another, serving cargo from a third, and secured by none of the above.

If the data about every container, its owner, its contents and its destination flows through a single operating system, then whoever controls that system sees the shape of the entire economy in real time.

Not a trade statistic from three months ago. The live feed.

That kind of information used to belong to spy agencies. Now it sits in a terminal control room next to a vending machine.

And here is the strange part. The most powerful infrastructure on Earth is also the least visible. You cannot walk into it. You cannot tour it. You cannot see it from a road. It sits behind fences and floodlights and is staffed by a few hundred people running ten thousand moving parts.

Power that is invisible is the most durable kind.

08 / THE FIGHT NOBODY WANTED TO WATCH

In October 2024, around forty-five thousand dockworkers on the American East and Gulf Coasts walked off the job. Ports from Maine to Texas went quiet. Analysts warned that every day of shutdown would take days to unwind afterward.

The headline demand was wages. The real battle was something else.

It was automation.

Workers understood a simple truth. Every driverless vehicle is a job that does not come back. Companies argued, with equal sincerity, that automation means safety, speed and competitiveness. Both sides were right, which is exactly what makes this kind of fight unwinnable by logic alone.

The strike lasted only a few days. The settlement that followed reportedly put hard limits on how far full automation can go at the covered terminals, for years.

Read that carefully. A union at a handful of ports negotiated a fence around a technology.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the Pacific, nobody was negotiating a fence.

That is the part nobody is saying out loud. Two systems. Two philosophies. One says: protect the jobs, accept a slower machine. The other says: build the machine, retrain the people later. Both have a body count of a kind. One counts lost jobs. The other counts lost competitiveness.

Neither will blink. And the box does not care either way.

I am not telling you which side is right. I am telling you that this is the argument of the next twenty years, and almost no one is having it in public.

09 / WHAT A ROBOT ACTUALLY SAVES

Let's be honest about the economics, because the hype version is wrong in both directions.

The pitch is easy. Machines cut labor costs, run around the clock, make fewer mistakes, and can be powered by electricity instead of diesel. Cleaner, safer, cheaper. Who could argue?

Reality is messier.

Studies and operator reports on automated terminals have shown mixed results. Some saw real gains in safety, predictability and emissions. Others saw productivity that lagged behind well-run manual terminals for years, because automation is not a switch you flip. It is a complete redesign of how a yard is laid out, how ships are sequenced, how trucks arrive, how software talks to hardware.

A robot is only as fast as the slowest thing it waits for.

If the ship is late, the robots wait. If the truck is late, the robots wait. If the customs system hiccups, the robots wait. If the crane is faster than the yard, the yard becomes the bottleneck, and the bottleneck simply moves one step down the line.

This is why the winners in this race are not the people who bought the shiniest vehicles. They are the people who got the whole system to flow, with software that sees the entire chain at once and moves before a problem happens, not after.

Cranes are commodities. Flow is the moat.

And flow is built from data. The terminals that learn fastest from every move they make will pull ahead of the ones that only own better steel. That is why the real arms race is not hardware. It is who has the most data and the best model of how a ship, a yard and a truck behave when everything goes slightly wrong.

10 / THE SHIP WITHOUT A CAPTAIN

If you think the dock is the end of the story, keep reading.

The biggest container ships today carry on the order of twenty-four thousand boxes. Lay those boxes end to end and you get a line well over a hundred and forty kilometers long. One vessel. One crew of a few dozen people.

Now zoom out. Shipping companies, classification societies and research labs have been testing autonomous and remotely supervised vessels for years. Small trial ships have already sailed with reduced crews or none on board. Nobody serious expects an unmanned megaship to cross an ocean tomorrow, and rules, insurance and liability are all miles behind the technology.

But look at the shape of the idea.

A port with no drivers. A ship with no helmsman. A supervisor in a control room who watches a hundred assets at once. A scheduling brain that decides which vessel gets which berth and which box rides which wheel.

Put those four pieces together and you get something we have never had: a global physical network that is managed like a data center.

In a data center, you do not ask where a given request is being processed. You do not care. You only care that the answer arrives. Packets in, packets out. The infrastructure disappears.

Now apply that to atoms. Boxes in, boxes out. The infrastructure disappears.

That is the endgame of the standard box. Not just cheaper freight. Freight that behaves like information.

11 / THE UNCOMFORTABLE MATH OF YOUR OWN LIFE

Let's make this personal, because that is where it gets weird.

Think about what is in your room right now. The phone. The charger. The shoes. The desk lamp. The t-shirt. The mug. Odds are high that a majority of it rode inside a steel box for part of its journey, and that some of that journey was handled by a machine no human was steering.

You have never met the system that delivered your life to your door.

You do not know its name. You cannot call its support line. You cannot vote on its design. And yet it shapes the price you pay, the week your order arrives, the jobs in your city, the cost of your groceries and the margin of the business you work for.

This is what mature infrastructure looks like. It becomes invisible precisely when it becomes essential. Nobody thinks about the water pipe until it bursts. Nobody thinks about the electrical grid until the lights go out.

The shipping network has been running so smoothly for so long that we forgot it was a choice.

It is not a law of nature that a sneaker from one side of the planet should cost less than a sandwich. That outcome was engineered. By boxes, by cranes, by software, by fuel, by a hundred thousand quiet decisions made by people you will never meet.

And what was engineered can be unengineered.

That is not a prediction. It is a reminder.

12 / WHAT TO WATCH FOR NEXT

If you want to see where this goes before everyone else does, stop reading headlines about ships and start watching five quieter signals.

Signal one: software, not steel. Watch which companies sell the operating systems that run terminals. Hardware gets copied in a few years. A system trained on a decade of real operations is much harder to copy.

Signal two: energy. Electric vehicles and shore power are turning ports into some of the largest industrial electricity customers in their regions. Whoever solves charging and grid load at scale solves a problem that every logistics hub will face.

Signal three: the last meter. The first company that automates the awkward manual tasks, the lashing, the inspections, the damaged-box handling, collapses the final human bottleneck. When that happens, the labor argument stops being theoretical.

Signal four: cyber defense. Every new connected machine is another door. Ports that treat security as an afterthought will learn the lesson the expensive way. Ports that treat it as a core function will quietly win contracts.

Signal five: politics. Rules about who may own, build and supply port technology are tightening in many countries. Infrastructure that used to be a matter for engineers is now a matter for ministers.

None of these will trend on a Tuesday afternoon. All of them will shape what you pay and what you can buy.

13 / THE THOUGHT EXPERIMENT

Try this.

Imagine you wake up tomorrow and every automated yard on Earth stops for a single week. No cranes, no vehicles, no scheduling brain. Just silence.

What happens?

Day one, nothing visible. Shelves are full. Stores have inventory. Life continues.

Day three, the first factories notice missing parts. Production lines slow. Managers start making calls.

Day five, ships pile up outside harbors. Insurance desks light up. Prices on certain goods start to twitch.

Day seven, the shock begins to reach people. Delays, shortages, bidding wars over whatever is left. And that is only the first week. The backlog would take weeks or months to clear, because a ship that misses its slot does not simply take the next one. It pushes everything behind it.

Now flip the experiment.

Imagine instead that the system works perfectly for the next fifty years. Costs fall. Speed rises. Emissions drop. Delivery times shrink. Prices stay low and everything just works.

What do we become?

A civilization that has handed its physical nervous system to machines it does not understand, run by systems it cannot audit, serving a population that forgot how any of it works.

Both futures are possible. Both are plausible. Which one we get depends on decisions being made right now, in rooms most of us will never enter, about technologies most of us have never heard of.

14 / THE PART THEY DON'T PUT IN THE PRESS RELEASE

Every automation story has a quiet middle chapter that never makes the brochure.

It is the chapter where the old experts retire, the new system takes over, and nobody is left who remembers how to do it by hand.

Pilots call it skill fade. When the machine flies the plane for years, the human forgets how to fly it. Then the day comes when the machine hands back the controls, usually in the worst possible moment, to someone who has not practiced in a decade.

Now translate that to a harbor. If the system fails, who still knows how to run a yard on paper, by radio, by instinct?

The smartest operators already ask that question and keep a small team that can. The rest are quietly hoping they never find out. Redundancy looks like waste right up until the morning it is the only thing standing between a calm shift and a national headline.

15 / THE LESSON UNDERNEATH ALL OF THIS

Strip away the cranes, the code, the strikes, the hackers and the geopolitics, and one idea remains.

Every great leap in productivity follows the same three steps.

First, someone standardizes something. A box. A plug. A protocol. A format.

Second, someone automates the standard. The more identical the thing, the easier it is to teach a machine to handle it.

Third, the automation becomes so reliable that society forgets it exists, and builds everything else on top of it.

That is how electricity worked. That is how the internet worked. That is how the shipping container worked. And that is how the next layer will work too, probably in places you are not looking.

The people who win these transitions are almost never the loudest. They are the ones who understood early that the boring layer underneath was the real prize.

So here is my challenge to you.

Next time you see a plain steel box on a truck, a train or a ship, do not see a box. See a standard. See a decision made seventy years ago that quietly rewired civilization. See a machine-readable object moving through a machine-run network toward a person who will never think about how it got there.

Then ask yourself the only question that matters.

What is the next box?

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Let me reframe this for you, Mr. Musk.
Could you please address the following concerns positively and transparently? If you can satisfactorily answer all these questions, I assure you that we, the people of India, will urge our government to welcome Starlink into our country.
1. Data Sovereignty and Security
What is Starlink's data policy? Where will Indian users' data be stored, and how will it be managed and protected?
Our position is simple: We cannot afford to have our citizens' data stored outside India's geographical boundaries.
2. National Security and Strategic Trust, As a massive global corporation providing services across multiple countries, how can we be assured that Starlink will never assist India's adversaries, particularly if diplomatic relations between India and the United States deteriorate?
What guarantees can you offer that our national security will never be compromised by foreign commercial or geopolitical interests?
3. Economic Dependence and Service Continuity. What happens if the Indian government has a disagreement with Starlink and the company decides to suspend, restrict, or disrupt its services?
Imagine Starlink capturing a significant share of India's telecom market, something you could potentially achieve through your enormous financial resources and marketing capabilities.
What guarantees do we have that Starlink will never use this market dominance to disrupt India's economy or pressure our government?
4. Sovereign Control Over Telecommunications
India must retain complete sovereign authority over telecommunications services operating within its territory.
As a country with an enormous and diverse population, we face unique internal security challenges. Sometimes, temporary internet restrictions become necessary to prevent the spread of misinformation or maintain public order.
Can Starlink guarantee that the Indian government will have the authority and technical capability to immediately restrict or suspend services in specific geographical areas whenever legally required?
We simply cannot afford a situation where our government must send a request to Starlink's headquarters in the United States and wait for approval before taking action within its own sovereign territory.
5. Affordability and Accessibility
India's average monthly telecom expenditure, including mobile calls and internet data, is approximately ₹300 (around $3.3).
Considering India's per capita income and the purchasing power of ordinary citizens, what is Starlink's pricing strategy?
How do you intend to make your services affordable for the vast majority of Indians, particularly the nearly 90% of the population that cannot reasonably afford expensive satellite internet subscriptions?
How will Starlink serve ordinary Indians rather than becoming a premium service accessible only to the wealthy? Mr. Musk, India is a democratic nation.
If you can address these five fundamental concerns with convincing explanations and concrete assurances, we will certainly urge our government to welcome Starlink to India.
We believe in globalization, international cooperation, technological progress, and fair competition, perhaps more strongly than many Western nations that frequently advocate these principles.
But globalization must never come at the expense of national sovereignty, economic independence, or the security of our citizens.
I sincerely hope you will respect the very democratic values and principles that the Western world so proudly champions.

Thank you.

Starlink isn't simply being “banned” by some anti-technology bureaucracy.

A satellite network isn't just another consumer app.

It can become part of:

📡 Communications
🛰️ Critical infrastructure
🛡️ National security
🚨 Emergency response
⚔️ Military operations

And when the network is controlled by a private company headquartered outside India, questions about data, lawful access, network control, security auditing and continuity during a crisis aren't optional.

They're the whole point.

Bring Starlink to India's villages.

Bring it to the islands.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
THE EMERGENCY OF 1975 WAS CONDEMNED AS A BLOT ON DEMOCRACY. ARE WE NOW WITNESSING THE EROSION OF DEMOCRACY WITHOUT A FORMAL DECLARATION OF EMERGENCY?

“इमरजेंसी को धब्बा बताने वालों ने लोकतंत्र को पूरी तरह तानाशाही में तब्दील कर दिया है। आज़ाद भारत के इतिहास में सबसे नाकाम सरकार और सबसे अलोकतांत्रिक प्रधानमंत्री का रिकॉर्ड बनने जा रहा है कल।”

The warning is stark: democracy can be weakened not only by declaring an Emergency, but also by restrictions that make fundamental rights increasingly difficult to exercise.

In the video, lawyers raise serious concerns about the extraordinary restrictions imposed in Delhi ahead of a planned peaceful protest. They question the closure of 57 Metro stations, reported transport disruptions, extensive security arrangements and the preparation of detention facilities. They also express concern that their plea was not being heard immediately by the Supreme Court. 

Their central argument is unmistakable:

“PEACEFUL PROTEST IS NOT UNLAWFUL.”

A democratic government has a legitimate responsibility to maintain public order and protect citizens. But that responsibility does not give it unlimited authority to restrict public movement, disrupt ordinary life or suppress peaceful dissent.

The constitutional question is one of necessity, proportionality and accountability.

WHEN THE ENTIRE CITY PAYS THE PRICE FOR A PEACEFUL PROTEST

If reports of extensive transport restrictions and preventive security measures are accurate, the authorities must explain why such measures were necessary, whether less restrictive alternatives were available, and how the rights of peaceful protesters and ordinary citizens were protected.

The lawyers in the video challenge the logic of shutting down an entire city because the authorities anticipate a protest. They argue that peaceful assembly cannot be treated as unlawful simply because it presents an administrative challenge. 

PUBLIC ORDER MUST NOT BECOME A BLANK CHEQUE FOR RESTRICTING CONSTITUTIONAL FREEDOMS.

The right to peaceful assembly and the freedom of speech are protected under Article 19 of the Indian Constitution, subject to constitutionally permissible restrictions. These freedoms are not absolute, but restrictions must satisfy the requirements of the Constitution and cannot be justified merely by administrative convenience.

AN UNDECLARED EMERGENCY? THE QUESTION DESERVES SERIOUS SCRUTINY

India's 1975 Emergency remains a warning about what happens when state power overwhelms democratic safeguards.

Today's circumstances should not automatically be equated with that period: a formal constitutional Emergency and restrictive measures imposed in anticipation of a protest are legally distinct.

Nevertheless, the absence of a formal Emergency declaration does not make every restriction on civil liberties acceptable.

When citizens struggle to assemble peacefully, journalists report alleged police excesses, and lawyers must urgently seek judicial intervention to protect fundamental rights, the appropriate response is not to silence criticism. It is to examine the facts, the legal basis for the restrictions and the safeguards available to affected citizens.

A DEMOCRACY MUST BE JUDGED NOT ONLY BY THE RIGHTS IT PROMISES, BUT ALSO BY HOW IT TREATS PEOPLE WHEN THEY EXERCISE THOSE RIGHTS.

THE HIGH COURTS AND THE SUPREME COURT MUST REMAIN EFFECTIVE GUARDIANS OF LIBERTY

The lawyers' appeal in the video underscores the importance of judicial independence and timely access to justice.

When restrictions threaten fundamental freedoms, courts must be able to examine their legality, necessity and proportionality. Citizens must have meaningful access to judicial remedies, particularly when the exercise of their constitutional rights is time-sensitive.

The rule of law requires both sides to be heard: authorities must be able to explain legitimate security concerns, and citizens must be able to challenge restrictions that may be excessive or unlawful.

A MESSAGE TO INDIA'S YOUTH

Do not allow the word Emergency to become merely a historical reference.

Remember the principles behind the struggle for democratic freedom: the right to question authority, the right to assemble peacefully, the independence of the judiciary, a free press and the accountability of those who exercise state power.

Do not confuse criticism of the government with hostility towards India. A government is temporary; the Constitution belongs to the Republic and protects its citizens.

Demand evidence. Demand transparency. Demand that restrictions be justified by law rather than political convenience.

And insist that allegations of unlawful restrictions or abuse of power be investigated impartially. Where wrongdoing is established, accountability must follow.

THE GOVERNMENT DOES NOT OWN THE STREETS. THE POLICE DO NOT OWN THE CONSTITUTION. AND NO POLITICAL LEADER OWNS THE REPUBLIC.

The people are entitled to ask difficult questions of those who govern them.

IF PEACEFUL PROTEST BECOMES IMPOSSIBLE, DEMOCRACY LOSES ONE OF ITS MOST IMPORTANT SAFEGUARDS.

Let India remain a country where dissent is protected, public order is maintained lawfully, and constitutional rights do not depend on the convenience of those in power.

NO UNLAWFUL RESTRICTIONS. NO IMPUNITY FOR ABUSE OF POWER. NO SILENCE IN THE FACE OF DEMOCRATIC EROSION.

🇮🇳 DEFEND THE CONSTITUTION. DEFEND PEACEFUL PROTEST. DEFEND DEMOCRACY.

JAI HIND!

text:
If India were a relatively small country like Bangladesh or Nepal, the kind of political activities that we are witnessing in India today, similar to those that preceded the fall of governments in Bangladesh and Nepal over the last two years, might already have led to a change of government here. 

However, India’s sheer size, its vast population and the fact that a large section of the population does not accept allegations of vote rigging, EVM manipulation or irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls have meant that the kind of civil disobedience witnessed in Dhaka and Kathmandu has not taken place on a comparable scale in India.

Since the Modi government came to power at the Centre in May 2014, 72 Assembly elections have been held across states and Union Territories. The BJP emerged as the largest party in only 31 of these elections, or around 43%. While the Opposition claims that elections are being rigged in favour of one particular party, and perhaps genuinely believes this to be the case, the electoral numbers do not support its claim. 

The government, as would be expected of any democratically elected government, has taken steps to prevent the kind of civil disobedience being attempted by the CJP, which has no formal status as a political party but is a group of protesters. The government is seeking to ensure that the protests do not create an opportunity to bring it down, as witnessed in Dhaka and Kathmandu, where similar street protests had ultimately led to the removal of democratically elected governments.

The Opposition has also questioned why central Delhi is being barricaded and metro services are being stopped. However, many of the journalists covering the protests today were also reporting during the demonstrations that followed the Nirbhaya rape case, when central Delhi was barricaded and metro stations were shut. This shows that governments take measures they consider necessary to maintain law and order, even when those measures restrict public movement.

Sections of the media are also amplifying the baseless narrative of CJP, for reasons best known to them.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text: NTRF/537/2026-SGST Dept. Can’t Hear Appeal Against CGST Order: Calcutta HC/ASP Private Limited versus Joint Commissioner of Revenue/Citation: JURISHOUR-3481-HC-2026(CAL)/Case No.: W.P.A. 19016 of 2025.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.
