Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Taxpayer Deposited Full Tax Demand within Due Time but Erroneously Credited IGST Instead of CGST and SGST: Madras High Court Holds Substantial Compliance Satisfied and Sets Aside Section 128A Waiver Rejection!

Issue:
Whether the Department can legally reject an application for waiver under Section 128A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, solely because the Assessee mistakenly deposited the admitted tax liability under the IGST head instead of the CGST and SGST heads, despite discharging the entire demand within the prescribed period.

Rule:
Exemption and waiver statutory provisions demand strict interpretation regarding substantive eligibility conditions, but substantial compliance suffices for procedural requirements, as laid down in Commissioner of Customs (Import), Mumbai v. Dilip Kumar & Company. Under Section 128A, the core substantive condition is the discharge of the "full amount of tax payable" under Section 73 within the stipulated time frame.

Application:
The Department passed an Order-in-Original against the Assessee on 30.12.2022. The Assessee duly discharged the entire tax liability through payments made on 27.03.2023 and 06.09.2024. However, owing to an inadvertent clerical error, an amount of ₹3,69,334/- was credited under the IGST head rather than the CGST and SGST heads, despite the Assessee having no IGST liability whatsoever. The Department rejected the waiver application under Section 128A on this solitary technicality. The Court observed that the substantive requirement of Section 128A—namely, timely receipt of the entire tax demand into the public exchequer—stood indisputably discharged. Because the deposit under the incorrect tax head was purely a clerical lapse and the revenue suffered no loss, the Assessee met the test of substantial compliance.

Conclusion:
Since the Assessee fulfilled the substantive condition of depositing the entire tax demand within time, hyper-technical procedural defects regarding accounting heads cannot disentitle a taxpayer to statutory relief. The High Court accordingly set aside the Department's rejection order and remanded the matter for fresh consideration within three months, directing the Assessee to complete the procedural formalities for crediting the amount under the appropriate heads.

Impact Analysis:
This decision prevents mechanical rejections under Section 128A, affirming that bona fide accounting head errors cannot defeat statutory waiver benefits once the entire tax demand has reached the government exchequer on time.

Contractor Denied Enhanced 18% GST Dues and Pending Bills of ₹65.88 Lakh by Government: Allahabad High Court Directs Department to Verify Dues and Issue Reasoned Decision Within One Month.s

Issue:
Whether a writ of mandamus could be issued directing the Department to release the outstanding payment of ₹65,88,416 along with interest, and whether the Department was obligated to consider the Assessee's representation for reimbursement of GST at the enhanced rate of 18% instead of 12% in light of the applicable government circulars.

Rule:
Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, a writ of mandamus lies to compel a public authority to perform a statutory or legal duty. When the tax burden under the Goods and Services Tax framework is enhanced by statutory notification/circular, the contract-awarding Department is under a legal obligation to verify such enhanced liability and pass a reasoned order regarding the differential tax payment within a reasonable time frame.

Application:
The Assessee executed work for the Department and deposited GST at the rate of 12%. Owing to a subsequent enhancement in tax rates pursuant to the Circular dated 18.07.2022, the tax became payable at the rate of 18%. The Department failed to release the principal dues amounting to ₹65,88,416 as well as the differential 6% GST amount. The Assessee filed a representation dated 25.04.2026 before the authorities, which remained unconsidered.
Relying upon the binding precedent in Writ Tax No. 42 of 2025, the Court noted that where the differential tax rate is claimed, the competent authority must verify the factual matrix and adjudicate upon the Assessee’s claim. Since the Department raised no objection to adopting the same procedure, the court found it fit to issue a time-bound administrative directive for verification.

Conclusion:
The High Court disposed of the writ petition by directing the Department (Opposite Party No. 2) to verify the facts concerning the Assessee's claim for reimbursement of GST at the enhanced rate of 18% (as against 12%) and to pass a reasoned decision in accordance with law within a strict timeline of one month.

Impact Analysis:
This judgment reinforces that government departments cannot indefinitely withhold statutory differential GST payments owed to contractors, mandating time-bound administrative verification and reasoned decisions on representations.

Facing massive tax demands over delayed ITC, vendor insolvency, and alleged short payment, Assessee secures major relief as Calcutta High Court quashes time-barred ITC demand under retrospective Section 16(5) and sets aside enhanced penalty.

Issue:
Whether the adjudication order passed under Section 73(9) of the CGST/WBGST Act, 2017—and the subsequent appellate orders upholding the tax demand and enhancing penalty—could be sustained where the demand for delayed ITC availment was covered by the retrospective insertion of Section 16(5), the ITC mismatch in GSTR-2A arose due to the supplier's insolvency proceedings, and the alleged short-paid tax had already been discharged voluntarily via Form GST DRC-03.

Rule:
Section 16(4) of the CGST/WBGST Act, 2017 restricts belated availment of input tax credit beyond the prescribed annual cut-off. However, Section 16(5), inserted retrospectively with effect from 1st July 2017, explicitly overrides this barrier, allowing registered taxpayers to claim ITC in respect of invoices or debit notes for Financial Years 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20, and 2020-21 in any return filed up to 30th November 2021. Further, Section 73(1) and Section 73(9) regulate determination of unpaid or short-paid tax and wrong ITC utilisation along with statutory penalties, while Section 107 governs statutory appeals before the appellate authority.

Application:
Chronological Factual Background On 31st January 2020, the Assessee deposited tax voluntarily through Form GST DRC-03 towards an alleged short payment of tax. On 6th July 2021, the Department issued a show cause notice under Section 73(1) alleging irregular availment and utilisation of ITC for Financial Year 2018-19 beyond the statutory deadline of Section 16(4), excess ITC claim for Financial Year 2017-18 due to reconciliation mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A after supplier Aircel went into insolvency and failed to upload returns, and short payment of GST for August 2017. On 25th October 2021, the Adjudicating Authority adjudicated all three issues against the Assessee, confirming a total demand of Rs. 19,02,986/- under Section 73(9) and levying a penalty of Rs. 1,00,000/- in Form GST DRC-07. On 22nd and 23rd March 2023, the Appellate Authority dismissed the Assessee's appeal and simultaneously allowed the Department's cross-appeal, enhancing the penalty to Rs. 3,80,597/- by applying the mandatory 10% statutory minimum under Section 73(9). Aggrieved by these orders, the Assessee approached the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

Conclusion:
The High Court set aside the original adjudication order as well as both appellate orders. The demand relating to delayed availment of ITC under Section 16(4) was quashed in view of Section 16(5). The remaining issues regarding GSTR-2A mismatch and alleged short payment, along with the consequential re-quantification of penalty, were remanded to the Adjudicating Authority for fresh adjudication on merits.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling reinforces that the retrospective benefit of Section 16(5) is absolute for pending litigations covering Financial Years 2017-18 to 2020-21, while clarifying that any departmental enhancement of penalty under Section 73(9) automatically collapses once the underlying tax demand is quashed or remanded for factual reverification.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Can Google be held liable for defamatory content on its platform?

The 2020 Supreme Court case Google India v. Visakha Industries tackled one of the most important questions in Indian cyber law: When does an intermediary lose its "safe harbour" protection? https://t.co/99am5RzgaH

The list of upcoming political cases is announced 

A list of 50 high-profile cases, which were filed under various fraud and corruption charges during the Ranil-Maithri administration and later suppressed due to political influence, has now resurfaced. This list, tabled in Parliament on the 8th by the Leader of the House, Minister of Transport, Highways and Urban Development, Bimal Rathnayake, includes over twenty politicians, members of political families, and numerous senior public officials.

Participating in the second reading debate on the Anti-Corruption (Amendment) Bill, the Minister emphasized that these cases were filed in the past based on evidence uncovered by institutions such as the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption and the Criminal Investigation Department. However, he pointed out that these cases, which were previously delayed through political deals, have now been expedited, and some are attempting to portray the punishment of offenders as political revenge.

According to the information presented by the Minister to Parliament, several prominent political figures have been accused in these cases filed from 2015 to date. Among them are Johnston Fernando (case filed on May 12, 2016, regarding a loss of Rs. 40 million by deploying Sathosa employees for political activities), Wimal Weerawansa (case filed on October 03, 2017, regarding the acquisition of illicit assets worth Rs. 75.4 million), Mahindananda Aluthgamage (case filed on August 18, 2016, concerning the issue of 14 carrom boards), and Basil Rajapaksa (case filed on April 15, 2015, regarding the misuse of Rs. 2,991 million from the Divinaguma fund for distributing aid during the presidential election).

In addition, the list includes cases filed at various times against individuals such as Rajitha Senaratne (financial loss incurred by leasing the Modara Fisheries Harbour), Ravi Karunanayake (loss of 51.9 billion in the 2016 Central Bank auction), Prasanna Ranatunga (threatening a businessman for Rs. 64 million), Priyankara Jayaratne, A.H.M. Fowzie, Sarana Gunawardena, Chamara Sampath Dasanayake, S.M. Ranjith Samarakoon, Piyasena Gamage, Bandula Gunawardena, Geetha Kumarasinghe, and Rohitha Bogollagama.

The Minister also revealed details about cases filed against several members of the Rajapaksa family. He cited as examples the cases filed against Namal Rajapaksa (Indian Krish project - July 01, 2016), Yoshitha Rajapaksa (acquiring Rs. 234 million through CSN channel - January 30, 2016), Gotabaya Rajapaksa (obtaining Rs. 33.9 million from the Land Reclamation and Development Corporation for the Medamulana monument - September 08, 2015), Shiranthi Rajapaksa (Siriliya Foundation and use of Defender vehicle related to Thajudeen murder - June 15, 2015), Rohitha Rajapaksa, Chamal Rajapaksa, Shashindra Rajapaksa, and Nirupama Rajapaksa.

Cases filed against former US Ambassador Jaliya Wickramasuriya (defrauding USD 332,000) and Udayanga Weeratunga, who was accused in the MiG aircraft deal, as well as senior state and police officials Lalith Weeratunga, Anusha Pelpita, Pujith Jayasundara, Hemasiri Fernando, Arjuna Mahendran, Arjun Aloysius, Kasun Palisena, Nalaka de Silva, Jayantha Wickramaratne, and Anura Senanayake, were also brought to attention in Parliament.

The Minister emphasized that investigative units have been strengthened and the judiciary is functioning, and that his government does not engage in revenge as past rulers did. He stated that there are no arbitrary arrests or a 'white van culture' today, unlike in the past.

Taking Rwanda, now known as the Singapore of Africa, and South Korea after 1997 as examples of progress achieved through anti-corruption efforts, Minister Bimal Rathnayake pointed out that investor confidence can be gained by raising international rankings through an independent judicial system where the law applies equally to all. text:
Can the Government suspend a political party’s Instagram handle without a clear statutory power? And can a politician boycott a courtroom while simultaneously asking the Supreme Court to transfer the same judge from hearing his case?  

This week, the Aam Aadmi Party raised both questions in two different constitutional courtrooms.  

In the Supreme Court, AAP challenged the suspension of its Gujarat unit’s Instagram handle, arguing that Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act was never meant to become a direct content-blocking weapon. 

Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat argued that the provision only deals with “safe harbour” obligations of intermediaries — not independent censorship powers.  The party says the move violates Article 19(1)(a), the constitutional guarantee of free speech. 

The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the Centre.  At the same time in the Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma appointed three amicus curiae for Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, and Satyendar Jain after the leaders chose to boycott proceedings, invoking “Mahatma Gandhi’s Satyagraha principles” and claiming their faith in the court process had been shaken.  

But here’s the constitutional twist: Kejriwal had also moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the excise policy case away from Justice Sharma’s bench — even as his legal team withdrew from participation before her court.  

This has now created a rare constitutional confrontation involving: 
⚖️ Article 19 vs state regulation of digital speech 
⚖️ Article 21 vs procedural fairness in criminal prosecution 
⚖️ Judicial recusal vs courtroom boycott 
⚖️ Free speech, due process, and strategic constitutional litigation  Justice Sharma’s response may become one of the most significant procedural moments in the case: instead of proceeding ex parte, she chose to appoint independent senior advocates as amicus curiae to preserve procedural fairness.  

And one line from the Supreme Court hearing may define this entire battle: “Today my portal is gone.”  Because this is no longer just about an Instagram account.

 It is about whether opposition parties in India can lose their digital voice overnight — and what constitutional remedy exists when that happens.

Fake videos of Delhi cops harassing girls were spreading online. Police say the footage was AI-generated, and a man is now under arrest.

The New Delhi district cyber police were monitoring social media when they noticed reels of alleged police harassment circulating. Their investigation traced the clips to an Instagram channel called News Ayina.

Police say Nadeem Ahmed, who runs it, confessed to making and sharing the deepfakes. An X post claims he was paid by political handlers to produce them. Police have not confirmed that part in the clip.

No leak, no hack. Just a believable fake of uniformed officers abusing women, built to spark outrage and push it to millions of phones before anyone checks. Once a video like that spreads, a correction rarely travels as far as the original.

The disturbing AI deepfake incident that has rightly angered our industry should not be looked at as an isolated incident.

It is a warning.

Ram Pothineni made an important point: “They’re faceless, so they’re fearless.” His suggestion of Aadhaar-linked accountability for online identities deserves serious discussion. Freedom of expression must always be protected. But anonymity cannot become a weapon to abuse, defame, sexually violate or deliberately destroy someone.

And this problem does not begin or end with deepfakes.

For quite some time, I have been concerned about organised and targeted negativity against films, actors and filmmakers within our own industry.

A film should succeed or fail because audiences watch it and decide. Criticism, reviews, trolling and disagreement are part of cinema today.

But a coordinated campaign to damage a film before audiences have even seen it is not criticism. It is sabotage.

Sundeep Kishan recently spoke publicly about targeted, paid negativity against him and his film even before its release. The Paradise had to approach a court before release seeking protection against defamatory and damaging content. These are not issues we should casually dismiss.

Behind every film are years of work, hundreds of families and producers risking enormous amounts of money.

Watch the film. Love it. Hate it. Criticise it brutally if you genuinely feel that way.

But first, LET THE FILM RELEASE.

What is even more unfortunate is that some of this comes from within our own ecosystem: fan groups fighting fan groups, anonymous pages pretending to be neutral, and accounts using photographs of actors as their DPs while behaving in ways those actors may never endorse.

What exactly are we achieving?

If one Telugu film loses, Telugu cinema does not win.

The cake is big enough for everyone to have a piece.

As President of the Movie Artistes Association, I want to make it clear that MAA is compiling information on accounts and networks repeatedly involved in targeted abuse and malicious campaigns, including accounts misusing actors’ photographs and identities to mislead people.

This is NOT about stopping criticism.

It is about accountability.

The present deepfake incident makes the larger conversation urgent. And unfortunately, this will not be the last deepfake. Technology is moving too quickly for us to believe deleting one video or filing one complaint solves the problem.

I request the Telugu Film Chamber, Producers Council, MAA and all stakeholders to sit together and create a permanent industry-wide mechanism to address AI deepfakes, impersonation, coordinated malicious campaigns and deliberate online sabotage.

Not another meeting that ends with a photograph.

Not another phone call.

A SYSTEM.

We may compete every Friday.

But we cannot spend the rest of the week trying to destroy one another.

Let audiences decide the fate of our films.

Let cinema win 🙏

Totally agree .. And the leverage is bigger than most people think.
India is the largest user base for WhatsApp, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook. Not a growth market. The base itself. Take India out and the  global user charts look very different.

But here's the uncomfortable part. We hold the users. They hold the rails, the data and the money.

Indian users generate the ad revenue. Indian creators make the content. The profits get booked somewhere else. We even had an equalisation levy to tax some of this. We dropped it last year. Quietly. Nobody asked what we got in return.

So the fight isn't about one tweet or one takedown order. It's about who owns the plumbing.

We've already shown we can build plumbing. UPI runs on public rails and private apps compete on top of it. Aadhaar, DigiLocker, ONDC, same idea. That's the template. Not bans. Rails.

The smarter play is slower and harder .. Data localisation with real teeth. Tax where the revenue is earned. Public rails where private monopolies sit today. 
Patient capital for Indian platforms that can actually scale. Doing nothing isn't neutral. It's a choice to stay a market and never become a maker.

Mandatory Reading for All CJP Members Joining the Protest 🇮🇳

Election Commission of India 🎯

1. What is it?
The Election Commission of India (ECI) is an independent body. It conducts elections in India. Its main job is to make sure elections are free and fair.

It was set up on 25 January 1950. This day is now National Voters’ Day.

Headquarters: Nirvachan Sadan, New Delhi.

2. Constitutional basis
The ECI gets its power from Article 324 of the Constitution.

Article 324 says the Commission has the superintendence, direction and control of:
- elections to Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha)
- elections to State Legislatures
- elections of the President and the Vice-President

Note: Local elections (panchayats and municipalities) are not done by the ECI. They are done by the State Election Commissions.

3. Composition
The Commission has three members:
- one Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)
- two Election Commissioners (ECs)

The CEC is the chairman. Decisions are taken by majority.

The President can also appoint Regional Commissioners to help during big elections, after talking to the Commission.

(As of 2026: Shri Gyanesh Kumar is the Chief Election Commissioner. Dr Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Dr Vivek Joshi are Election Commissioners.)

4. Appointment
The President appoints the CEC and the Election Commissioners.

Under the 2023 law, a Selection Committee recommends the names. The committee has:
- the Prime Minister
- a Union Cabinet Minister chosen by the Prime Minister
- the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the largest opposition party)

5. Term and removal
- Term: 6 years, or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
- They cannot be reappointed to the same post.
- The CEC can be removed only in the same way as a Supreme Court judge (by Parliament, with a special majority).
- Other Election Commissioners can be removed only on the recommendation of the CEC.
- Their salary and conditions cannot be changed to their disadvantage after appointment.

6. Main functions
- Prepare and revise the electoral rolls (voter lists).
- Conduct elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.
- Decide the election schedule and polling dates.
- Recognise political parties as national or state parties.
- Allot election symbols to parties and candidates.
- Enforce the Model Code of Conduct during elections.
- Cancel polls if there is booth capturing, violence, or other serious problems.
- Advise the President or Governor on disqualification of members (for example, under the anti-defection law in some cases).
- Register political parties.

7. Important powers
- It can supervise the whole election process.
- It can give directions to election officers.
- It can use government staff for election work (Article 324(6)).
- It can postpone or cancel an election in a constituency if the situation is not fair.
- It monitors election spending and can take action against violations.

8. Why it is independent
- Fixed term and security of tenure.
- Removal of the CEC is difficult (same as a Supreme Court judge).
- Conditions of service cannot be reduced after appointment.
- It does not work under any ministry during elections.

9. Quick facts to remember
- Constitutional body under Article 324.
- Started: 25 January 1950.
- Multi-member body since 1993 (CEC + 2 ECs).
- Does not conduct panchayat or municipal elections.
- Motto idea: free, fair and transparent elections.
- Helpline: 1950.

1. Strengthening the Independence of the Election Commission
a) Transparent appointments: Consider a broad-based selection mechanism involving the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India, or another suitably balanced arrangement, to strengthen the impartiality and credibility of appointments.

2. Transparency and Accountability in Electoral Rolls
a) Safeguards against wrongful deletion: Ensure a verifiable audit trail for deletions, prior individual notice, an opportunity to respond and an accessible appeal mechanism.

3. Transparency in Election Campaigns and Political Funding
a) Public funding: Examine suitable models of public funding or publicly supported election resources to reduce the undue influence of wealthy donors and corporate interests.

What's missing is a timeline. The government hasn't said when the security review will finish, for Starlink or for anyone else.

Starlink just told India it's ready to launch, pending final government approvals. Here's what you need to know.

Lauren Dreyer, SpaceX's Vice President of Starlink Business Operations, spoke at India Mobile Congress in New Delhi today. She thanked the Government of India and the Department of Telecommunications for the chance to share Starlink's vision. Her message: "We stand ready to serve India, as soon as India is ready!"

Starlink says it has spent the past five years working with Indian regulators, industry and operators. The goal was to adapt its operations to serve India, and to meet Indian security needs. It says it can help reach places where the last mile is still the hardest mile, working alongside India's operators, government and industry. It also says it can help accelerate efforts to connect India 100%.

The ground work is done. Starlink has built 20 gateway sites in India, with hundreds of antennas. It has security controls tailored to Indian requirements. Indian user data will stay within the country.

The remaining step is government authorisation. Under the DoT's current authorisation terms, satellite communication operators must also pay an annual licence fee of 8% of AGR.

Reaction is split. Some investors see India as a huge market for Starlink. Some critics want it banned, citing security fears.

Key numbers:
- 20 gateway sites built in India
- Hundreds of antennas installed
- 5 years working with Indian regulators
- 8% of AGR annual licence fee for satcom operators

A road safety officer stopped us today. My brother was driving, and he presented his valid UAE/Dubai driving licence. The vehicle papers were checked everything was intact. Fire extinguisher? Intact. Warning triangle? Intact. Spare tyre? Intact.

The officer then demanded a Nigerian driver's licence. My brother explained that we don't reside in Nigeria and had only just returned. The officer insisted that a Dubai licence could not be used in Nigeria, even for one day.

I simply asked him to show us the specific law we had violated. Instead of showing the law, the attitude changed. He started saying I was claiming to know everything and that "this is Nigeria."

I also explained that my own Nigerian driver's licence has expired because I no longer drive in Nigeria. I told him I have not driven since I returned and have no intention of renewing a licence for a vehicle I am not driving. He insisted that even if I don't drive, I must renew it.

I asked him: Why should I keep spending money renewing a driver's licence when I have decided not to drive in Nigeria? And why are citizens constantly being suffocated with one charge, renewal or demand after another?

I even asked whether he understood that citizens have constitutional rights and should not be treated as if every interaction with a government officer must end in intimidation or payment. He simply looked at me as though I was the one who had lost my mind.

What made it worse was seeing a condemned truck that clearly should not have been on the road pass right in front of us without being stopped, while we were being held over a valid foreign driver's licence.

When I questioned the double standard, the situation escalated. I made a phone call, and the officer accused me of calling "cultists" to attack them.

The next thing, a JTF team comprising soldiers, police and civil defence arrived aggressively, shouting for everyone to come down from the vehicle. We were three people—my brother, his wife and me. His wife was still inside the vehicle.

They aggressively tried to take my phone when I was recording what was happening. I asked them to first hear our side of the story.

After they eventually listened and confirmed what had happened, we were told to leave and not be aggressive towards officers. But I never came there looking for trouble. I was simply asking questions and trying to document what was happening to us.

They later insisted that I delete the video, which I did in their presence.

Why all this suffocation of citizens?

Why must asking a legitimate question to a government officer suddenly become "insulting an officer," "knowing too much," or "challenging authority"?

Respect for citizens and respect for personnel must work both ways. A uniform is not a licence to intimidate citizens, and citizens should not have to surrender their rights simply because someone in uniform says, "This is Nigeria."

Say NO to citizens' intimidation.

I will never bow to intimidation or oppression.

text:
I’m finna burn that bitch .... Dumpster Murder Weapon Used to Kill Troy Pouncey Sold to Feds, Chicago Felon Levion Thomas Gets 15 Years

United States v. Levion Thomas Case No. 23 CR 184

by @drkugler https://t.co/MPWurl9uLk® 
Crime Report Oct 7, 2026

CHICAGO — A Chicago felon who federal prosecutors say used a 9mm handgun to kill Troy Pouncey, threw the murder weapon into a dumpster when police closed in, returned 20 minutes later to retrieve it and ultimately sold the same gun to an undercover federal agent has been sentenced to 15 years in federal prison.

Levion Thomas, 31, pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm, not murder. But federal prosecutors presented evidence at sentencing that they said established Thomas used the same Smith & Wesson M&P Shield 9mm pistol to kill 31-year-old Troy Pouncey on March 5, 2023.    

Thomas was indicted April 13, 2023, on one federal count of being a felon in possession of a firearm. He later pleaded guilty to that charge. Prosecutors used Pouncey's killing as relevant conduct at sentencing and sought the statutory maximum 15-year sentence.     

“You Got 9 Shells? New Opponents.”

Pouncey was shot at approximately 2:14 p.m. March 5, 2023, at 7115 S. Calumet Ave.

Federal prosecutors said three masked gunmen fired multiple shots at Pouncey before fleeing in a red Chevrolet Sonic.

Investigators said Thomas had been seen driving the same vehicle numerous times.

Cell tower records also placed a phone associated with Thomas in the general vicinity of the homicide a little more than an hour before Pouncey was killed.     

But prosecutors said evidence of the conflict began before the shooting.

Approximately four hours before Pouncey was killed, Thomas allegedly texted a confidential informant:

“You got 9 shells? New opponents.”

Prosecutors argued the request for 9mm ammunition showed Thomas was preparing for the confrontation that ended with Pouncey's death.     

The government's sentencing memorandum describes additional conversations involving ammunition, retaliation and an ongoing conflict after Pouncey was killed.

Taken together, the evidence described by federal prosecutors points to an ongoing armed street conflict rather than a random encounter. The available federal records, however, do not establish which gang or gangs, if any, were involved.

“Delete That Last Message”

The day after Pouncey was killed, prosecutors said Thomas sent the confidential informant a screenshot of a news article reporting Pouncey's death.

Then came another message:

“Delete that last message.”

Investigators were also recording conversations between Thomas and the informant.

During a March 7 call, the informant asked Thomas about a jacket.

Thomas responded:

“That Tommy Hilfiger? Boy that bitch, I’m finna burn that bitch.”

Thomas also discussed ammunition and possible retaliation, according to the government's sentencing memorandum.

He told the informant he had been monitoring the Citizen app and indicated he believed law enforcement did not know what was happening.

Thomas also claimed he had been in Gary at an Airbnb.     

Murder Weapon Goes Into a Dumpster

Police found the red Chevrolet Sonic on March 11.
Federal prosecutors said Thomas fled and later returned to the parking lot, where he threw a firearm into a dumpster.

But he apparently had second thoughts.

Thomas returned approximately 20 minutes later and retrieved the handgun from the dumpster.     

The following day, Thomas was recorded telling the informant:

“I ain’t going to lie to you, I’m scared bro.”

Thomas then referred to authorities taking the red Chevrolet.

“I can’t tell you where I’m going but look they came and took her car man, I’m gone.”     sentencimng doc show_temp

Thomas had recovered the gun from the dumpster.
Eight days later, according to prosecutors, he sold it.

He Sold the Gun to the Feds

On March 20, Thomas met a confidential informant and an undercover law enforcement officer in a strip mall parking lot in Burnham, Illinois.

Thomas handed over a Smith & Wesson M&P Shield 9mm semiautomatic pistol.

Federal ballistics testing determined it was the same firearm used to kill Troy Pouncey two weeks earlier, according to prosecutors.     

The transaction was recorded.

Thomas warned the undercover buyer:

“Be careful with that man. That, that motherfucker there (unintelligible) that motherfucker there, you point it’s gonna go.”

Thomas then allegedly described what happened when the gun was fired at a person:

“That shit fucked me up (unintelligible). I ain’t gonna lie to you. You ain’t hit him in the head. First one hit him, boom. Second one. All left side. Tore his ass up. Bet.”

The federal transcript records Thomas describing the shots:

“First one hit him, boom. Second one. All left side. Tore his ass up.”     

Those statements became particularly significant when investigators compared Thomas' description with Pouncey's wounds.

The medical examiner found Pouncey had been shot in the left side of his head, left side of his neck and multiple times in his left side, back and arm, according to prosecutors.     

Federal prosecutors argued Thomas' recorded description corresponded with Pouncey's actual wounds.

Then there was the physical evidence.

Ballistics linked the gun Thomas sold to the undercover officer directly to the gunfire that killed Troy Pouncey.    

Thomas Claimed Self Defense

Thomas suggested the shooting involved self defense.
Federal prosecutors rejected that explanation.

The government pointed to Thomas' alleged request for 9mm ammunition hours before the killing, his conduct after Pouncey's death and his repeated attempts to dispose of the firearm.

Prosecutors argued fleeing, throwing the gun into a dumpster, retrieving it and later selling it were inconsistent with someone who believed he had lawfully acted in self defense.    

History of Gun Cases Before Pouncey's Killing

Thomas' involvement with firearms did not begin with the Pouncey case.

Chicago Police arrest records supplied for Thomas show multiple contacts with police dating to 2017, including arrests involving weapons.

The federal sentencing memorandum goes further because it documents convictions rather than merely arrests.

Federal prosecutors calculated Thomas at criminal history category V with 10 criminal history points.
His record included a 2017 firearm possession conviction, three retail theft convictions, a 2019 aggravated assault conviction and two aggravated unlawful use of a weapon convictions.    

Prosecutors argued previous sentences had failed to deter Thomas and that his conduct involving firearms had escalated.     

Then came March 2023

Hours before Pouncey was killed, prosecutors say Thomas was asking for 9mm ammunition for “new opponents.”

After Pouncey was killed, prosecutors say Thomas discussed retaliation, talked about burning a jacket, tried to dispose of the gun and ultimately sold it to an undercover officer.

Ballistics tied that gun to Pouncey's killing.

15 Years Without a Murder Conviction

Thomas was not convicted of murdering Pouncey.
His federal conviction was for being a felon in possession of a firearm.

But the homicide dramatically changed his federal sentencing calculation.

The federal probation calculation placed Thomas at an offense level of 35 and criminal history category V. The resulting guideline range was 262 to 327 months.
The firearm offense carried a statutory maximum of 180 months, making 15 years the effective advisory sentence.     

Prosecutors asked for all 180 months.    
The government wrote:
“Too many people in this city believe that they can unlawfully possess firearms with impunity. This needs to stop.”     sentencimng doc show_temp

Parts of Federal Case Sealed

Parts of the federal case were sealed or subject to restrictions.

The original March 30, 2023 criminal complaint against Thomas was filed UNDER SEAL. It accused Thomas of illegally possessing the Smith & Wesson M&P Shield 9mm he allegedly sold in Burnham on March 20.     

Federal prosecutors later sought an unopposed protective order governing sensitive discovery, citing law enforcement interests and the privacy of third parties.     

At least one exhibit referenced in the government's sentencing memorandum was also filed under seal because it identified an uncharged individual.     

The public federal record nevertheless lays out the government's trail.

Request for 9mm ammunition hours before Pouncey was killed.

Phone associated with Thomas near the scene.

Red Chevrolet linked to the gunmen's escape.

message about Pouncey's death followed by an instruction to delete it.

discussion about burning a jacket.

firearm thrown into a dumpster and retrieved 20 minutes later.

recorded gun sale to an undercover officer.
Thomas' own recorded description of a shooting.
Wounds prosecutors said corresponded with that description.

ballistics tying the gun Thomas sold to Pouncey's killing.

Thomas tried to get rid of the gun more than once.
The last time, he sold it to the feds.

Report Image Caption

Federal prosecutors say Levion Thomas used a Smith & Wesson 9mm to kill Troy Pouncey, later threw the gun into a dumpster before retrieving it, and ultimately sold the same firearm to an undercover federal agent. During the recorded sale, Thomas allegedly described the shooting and warned the buyer about the gun: “You point it’s gonna go.” Federal ballistics testing linked the firearm Thomas sold to Pouncey's killing.

Illegal Infiltration & Fake Documentation:-A Real Case I Handled

Home Minister @AmitShah ji has held that the population of Muslims in India has increased due to illegal infiltration. Let me share a real case I personally handled about 5–6 years ago in Mumbai, one among many that reveal how deep this problem runs. Please do read to understand the rot.

1. The Client’s Request:- One evening after court hours, a Muslim gentleman known to me came to my office. He had given his premises in Govandi, Mumbai, on a leave and license agreement to a family of 6/7 people.
Even after the agreement expired, the family refused to vacate.

I perused his papers and assured him of appropriate legal action. He then asked if the matter could be resolved sooner than usual.
When I explained that such cases typically take little time, he hesitated and what he said next stunned me.

2. The Shocking Revelation :- He quietly said, “Sir, those tenants are not Indians, they are Bangladeshis.”

That single sentence changed everything. Two thoughts struck me instantly:
1. Why hadn’t he mentioned this earlier?
2. How did they even get valid Aadhaar and PAN cards as visible in the agreement?

3. The Investigation:- On examining the documents, everything looked perfectly legitimate; Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, even voter ID.
We filed RTIs, involved the local police, and began to dig deeper.

Gradually, the truth surfaced, the birth certificate forming the basis of all these documents was forged.

Using that single forged certificate from 1967, the accused had created a full legal identity for himself and his family, including Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, and voter ID.

4. A Web of Fraud:- It didn’t stop there. The man had used the same method to obtain documents for his wife and children. His son was even married to an Indian Muslim woman, effectively merging into the Indian population.

During the investigation, we uncovered an organized network, a full-fledged industry operating to regularize illegal immigrants by manufacturing fake Indian identities that pass every verification test.

5. The Larger Problem:-India’s diversity makes such infiltration even easier. People entering from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, or Nepal often resemble locals making visual identification almost impossible.

Add to this the corruption that exists from border checkpoints to administrative offices, and you have a perfect ecosystem for illegal population growth.

In this very case, we found the involvement of certain officials, and shockingly, even a few lawyers.

6. A Moment That Exposed the Rot:- One of those lawyers, representing the Bangladeshi accused, told my Muslim junior,
“How can you do this? This is a matter of religion.”
My junior stood firm and warned him of a complaint before the Bar Council.

This single moment revealed how some individuals, blinded by religious or political motives, are actively protecting those who illegally enter and settle in India.

7. The Unanswered Question:- 
This wasn’t the only case, I have come across several similar ones.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

To,
The Chief Architect,
New Delhi Municipal Council,
New Delhi.
chief.architect@ndmc.gov.in
Sub: Objections qua the proposed removal of the Masjid Sunehri Bagh Road Roundabout, New Delhi 110011.
Sir,
I am concerned with your notice published in various Newspapers dated 24.12.2023. I am a practicing Muslim and I have a right to offer prayer in every Mosque, hence, I am an interested person as defined under Section 3(k) of the Waqf Act, 1995. Being a person interested in the captioned mosque, I am clearly interested in its protection and preservation.
As per my observations on the ground, the proposed removal of the captioned mosque on the premise that the MCD has received a reference from the Delhi Traffic Police for providing traffic engineering proposal for providing sustainable mobility in the vicinity of roundabout of Sunehri Bagh is only an excuse to remove the subject mosque. Neither the Traffic Police has asked for removal nor is the entire roundabout occupied by the said Mosque. As a matter of fact, not more than 10% of the roundabout is occupied by the said mosque, rest of the roundabout is occupied by the assets of Delhi Metro Rail Corporation, a park and other sundry things including a telecom tower.
The subject mosque is significant not only from the religious point of view but also for historical, political and cultural reasons.
As a religious center it is significant because Muslim Members of Parliament, members of Muslim community working in various government offices visit this mosque for the purpose of worship and to offer five times compulsory prayers, daily.
It is a historical place because it is more than 150 years old and has survived British Raj also.
It is politically significant because eminent Freedom Fighter and activist Syed Fazl-ul-Hasan used to stay at this mosque when he was participating in Constituent Assembly’s meetings as a member of Constituent Assembly. It is him who gave the slogan of ‘इन्किलाब ज़िंदाबाद’. He was elected to the Constituent Assembly from the United Provinces on a Muslim League Ticket. After partition, he was one of the 28 members of the Muslim League who remained in India and attended the meetings of the Constituent Assembly.
Syed Fazl-ul-Hasan, who is famous by pen-name ‘Hasrat Mohani’ [Mohani because he was from Mohan] was, besides being an activist and freedom fighter, was a world famous poet. ‘चुपके चुपके रात दिन आंसू बहाना याद है’ a world famous rendition by Ghulam Ali, ‘कैसे छुपाऊं राज़ ए ग़म’, ‘भुलाता लाख हूँ लेकिन’ and other master class renditions by late Ustad Mehdi Hazan Khan Sahab and ‘रौशन जमाल ए यार से है अंजुमन तमाम’ a melodious rendition by the King of Ghazals late Jagjit Singh sahib are the few Ghazals penned by Hasrat Mohani sahib. Beyond that, Hasrat Mohani used to carry with him a flute and was skilled flute player. He had also written various Nazms on Shri Krishna. For example his two famous Nazms are ‘मोसे छेर करत नन्दलाल’ and ‘मथुरा कि नगर है आशिकी का’. This makes the subject mosque culturally significant.
In any other country, such a place would have been preserved at the expenses of the State, however, it is unfortunate that New Delhi Municipal Council is trying to erase such a multidimensional place, that too without being backed by any empirical data.
This mosque is also one of the 123 Waqf Properties which are the subject matter of litigation between the Delhi Waqf Board and the Union of India. There are two Writ Petitions, WPC no. 1961 of 2022 and WPC no. 2686 of 2023 are pending before the Hon’ble Delhi High Court. In WPC no. 2686 of 2023, vide the order dated 26.04.2023 the Hon’ble High Court recognized the administration and management of those 123 waqf properties by the Delhi Waqf Board and permitted the Union of India to ‘carryout inspection while ensuring minimal disruption in the day-to-day administration of the subject properties by the petitioner’. The administration of the property presupposes the existence of the property. Hence, it becomes duty of not only the Union of India but also every agency to ensure that the properties subject matter of the Delhi Waqf Board’s WPC no. 2686 of 2023 continue to exist. This applies to the New Delhi Municipal Council also.
That there is no difficulty with the traffic movement around this roundabout. The traffic is not around this roundabout.
Hence, the alleged traffic congestion is nothing but a ruse to target this Mosque, which I oppose.
Thank you,

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

According to an official notice dated 10 June 2026, the Commission has taken cognizance of a representation submitted by Asem Roshan Singh on 22 May 2026. The petition raises concerns regarding the reported abduction and hostage-taking of Naga tribal civilians in Manipur.

The notice, issued by the NCST under its constitutional powers conferred by Article 338A of the Constitution of India, directs the Chief Secretary and the DGP to furnish the facts of the case and details of the action taken within 30 days from the date of receipt of the notice.

The Commission stated that the matter has been accepted for investigation/inquiry. It further noted that if no reply is received within the stipulated period, it may exercise the powers of a Civil Court available to it under Article 338A of the Constitution and issue summons for the appearance of the concerned authorities or their representatives.

The notice has been signed by Kushal Dev Verma, Deputy Secretary, National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, and a copy has also been forwarded to the petitioner, Asem Roshan Singh.

The issuance of the notice indicates that the Commission has initiated the process of seeking information from the concerned authorities. The notice itself does not record any findings on the allegations, and the matter remains under examination by the Commission pending receipt of the reports from the Government of Manipur and the Manipur Police.
